0.title: One Church, Many Traditions
0.essay:
There is one holy, catholic and apostolic church. Yet across twenty centuries that one church has expressed itself in a remarkable variety of traditions, each preserving something precious, and each bearing the marks of human frailty.

Why tour the traditions?

This study visits thirteen Christian families: Presbyterian and Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist, Brethren, Pentecostal and Charismatic, Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Anabaptist and Mennonite, Congregationalist, Oriental Orthodox and Seventh-day Adventist.

The aim is not comparative religion but pastoral wisdom. Your congregation almost certainly contains believers shaped by several of these traditions. Understanding where they have come from — what they love, what questions shaped them, which texts they have cherished — is an act of love. It also deepens our wonder at what Christ purchased: a people drawn from every tribe, tongue and tradition.

Charity and clarity

We approach each tradition charitably. Where a tradition holds to the apostolic faith — the Trinity, the full deity and humanity of Christ, the authority of Scripture, salvation by grace — we recognise brothers and sisters. Where there are serious departures from Scripture, we name them clearly but without contempt. We do not pretend that all differences are trivial; they are not. But we seek to understand before we evaluate, and to honour what God has done through each stream, even as we hold our own Reformed convictions with gratitude.

Reformed theology is our home. But home is the place from which you can travel generously and return wisely.

How each chapter runs

Each chapter tells where a tradition came from, what it believes and loves, the Scriptures it has especially treasured, where we differ, and the people who show it at its best. The chapters can be read in any order, perhaps when you meet someone from that tradition.

1.title: Presbyterian & Reformed
1.essay:
The Presbyterian and Reformed tradition traces its roots to John Calvin’s Geneva and John Knox’s Scotland, and to the great confessions of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, above all the Westminster Confession of Faith (1646) and its Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Further back still, it stands on Augustine, who laboured to show that salvation is wholly from God.

Three defining marks

First, covenant theology: the Bible is read as the unfolding story of God’s covenants, with Christ as the head of a new humanity. Second, the doctrines of grace: God’s sovereign election, Christ’s definite atonement, the Spirit’s effectual call and the perseverance of the saints. Third, the regulative principle of worship: in gathered worship we do what Scripture commands, not what tradition or taste permits.

Underneath them all stand the five solas of the Reformation — Scripture alone, grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, to the glory of God alone. They are not slogans but load-bearing walls.

Elders

Government is by elders (Greek presbyteroi) — teaching elders, who are ministers, and ruling elders — accountable through a ladder of courts: session, presbytery and general assembly. Calvin believed this structure guards against both papal tyranny and congregational anarchy. Paul’s charge to the Ephesian elders is its charter: “Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28). Notice the plural. A group of elders, accountable to one another, care for a flock that is not theirs but God’s. Every elder should read that verse on his knees.

Treasured texts

The tradition rests its confidence in Scripture on 2 Timothy 3:16: “All Scripture is breathed out by God.” Through the personalities and vocabularies of human writers, the Spirit ensured that what they wrote is what God intended to say, and it is enough: no supplementary teaching office or new revelation is needed.

It reads election not as a cold decree but as a love letter written before the world began: God “chose us in him before the foundation of the world … In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons” (Ephesians 1:4–5). And it rests on the golden chain: “those whom he predestined he also called, and those whom he called he also justified, and those whom he justified he also glorified” (Romans 8:30). Every link holds, not because of our grip on God but because of his grip on us.

Sacraments

There are two, baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Presbyterians baptise believers and their children, as the sign of the covenant. The Supper is a real means of grace: Christ is truly present by the Spirit and received by faith, but not in the physical bread and wine — against both Rome’s transubstantiation and the Lutheran presence “in, with and under” the elements. (This app’s own studies, while Reformed in theology, hold to believer’s baptism; see the studies on the Church and Covenant Theology.)

Worship and preaching

A Presbyterian service typically runs: call to worship, confession of sin and assurance of pardon, Scripture readings, singing of psalms and hymns, prayer, sermon, the Lord’s Supper (weekly in some congregations) and benediction. Nothing is filler; every element is drawn from Scripture’s pattern.

The Shorter Catechism’s first answer frames the whole Christian life: “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.” Glory and enjoyment are not in tension; as Jonathan Edwards and John Piper have taught, we most enjoy God when we most glorify him, and most glorify him when we most enjoy him.

Its great preachers have shaped the English-speaking church: John Knox, George Whitefield, Thomas Chalmers, J. Gresham Machen, Martyn Lloyd-Jones, R. C. Sproul, Sinclair Ferguson, Alistair Begg and Tim Keller — and, though a Baptist, the deeply Reformed Charles Spurgeon. They show that Reformed theology, far from being cold, produces preaching of great warmth and depth.

For reflection

Which of the three marks — covenant, grace, regulated worship — shapes your own church most? Why does a plurality of accountable elders matter? How does the Shorter Catechism’s first answer change the way you think about joy?

2.title: Lutheran
2.essay:
On 31 October 1517 an Augustinian monk posted ninety-five theses on the door of the Castle Church in Wittenberg. Martin Luther had not meant to found a new church. He meant to call the church back to the gospel he had rediscovered in Romans: the righteousness of God is not the standard that condemns us but the gift that saves us.

The tower

“For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith for faith, as it is written, ‘The righteous shall live by faith’” (Romans 1:17). For years Luther read “the righteousness of God” as divine wrath, God’s demand that crushed him. Then he saw that it is not what God demands but what God gives. “I felt that I was altogether born again,” he wrote, “and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” The verb “revealed” is present tense: every time the good news is announced, the gift of God’s righteousness is held out again to the empty-handed sinner.

Paul labours the point almost comically, as if he knows we will try to smuggle in a contribution: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Luther’s great discovery was that faith is not a work that earns grace; it is the posture of the soul that receives it.

Law and gospel

Where Reformed theology stresses God’s sovereignty and the covenant structure of redemption, Lutheranism puts the distinction between law and gospel in the foreground. The law is God’s demand: it shows what we owe and what we lack, reveals sin, crushes pride and drives us to despair. The gospel is God’s gift: it announces the free forgiveness of sins won by Christ and received by faith alone. Confusing them — adding conditions to the gospel, or turning it into a new law — is, Lutherans say, the root of error. The preacher’s task is to kill with the law and raise with the gospel.

So the great Lutheran text is Romans 8:1: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.” Not reduced, not deferred — none. Luther had spent years in a monastery trying to silence his conscience with penance. The gospel dethroned that tyrant, not by saying sin does not matter but by saying Christ has borne it all.

Justification

Later Lutherans called justification the article on which the church stands or falls. God declares the sinner righteous because Christ’s righteousness is credited to him by faith. It is forensic, external and complete: not the beginning of a process of becoming righteous, as Rome teaches, but an instant declaration. On this, Lutherans and Reformed stand side by side.

Liturgy and the Supper

Lutherans keep a high view of liturgy and the church calendar, believing that ancient forms of worship, cleansed of medieval additions, are a gift rather than a burden. The Lord’s Supper is central and frequent. Lutherans teach that Christ’s body and blood are truly present “in, with and under” the bread and wine — distinguished carefully from Rome’s transubstantiation, and often called “consubstantiation” by others, though Lutherans reject the term. Infant baptism is kept, understood as a means by which God creates and sustains faith.

When Luther debated Zwingli at Marburg in 1529 and Zwingli urged a figurative reading of “This is my body”, Luther chalked the Latin words on the table: Hoc est corpus meum. Whether or not his formulation is finally the most defensible — the Reformed view differs — his instinct was godly. Jesus, “the bread of life” (John 6:35), gives himself to his people in the Supper.

Luther’s wider legacy

Beyond justification, Luther left the church the theology of the cross, the doctrine of vocation (all lawful work is a sacred calling), the two-kingdoms framework (church and state as distinct realms of God’s rule), and a hymn-singing tradition that gave us “A Mighty Fortress Is Our God”.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, executed by the Nazis in 1945, distinguished cheap grace — forgiveness without repentance, grace without discipleship — from costly grace, which cost God his Son and costs the believer his old life. His warning was aimed at a Lutheranism that had become careless, using grace as an excuse. The law still kills and grace truly gives life; but the forgiven sinner follows Christ.

For reflection

How would you explain the difference between law and gospel? Where are you tempted to turn the gospel into a new law? What can Reformed Christians learn from Lutheran joy in the Supper, even where we differ on how Christ is present?

3.title: Anglican & Episcopal
3.essay:
The Church of England was born in the sixteenth century where royal politics met genuine Reformation conviction. Henry VIII’s break with Rome in 1534 was political. The theological Reformation that followed was real, led by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, who gave the church the Book of Common Prayer (1549, 1552) and the Thirty-Nine Articles (1563).

A middle way

Anglicanism has always seen itself as a via media, a middle way — not between Protestantism and Catholicism, but between the excesses of both: the rigidity of Geneva and the authoritarianism of Rome. Richard Hooker’s Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity (1593) argued that church order should be shaped by Scripture, tradition and reason, later pictured as a three-legged stool. This has made Anglicanism theologically roomy — sometimes admirably so, sometimes to the point of incoherence.

The Articles

At its confessional core, Anglicanism is evangelical. Article XI says that “we are justified by Faith only”, in agreement with Lutheran and Reformed conviction, and Articles IX to XVII treat original sin, free will, justification and predestination in robustly Protestant, substantially Reformed language. Much of modern Anglican diversity is a departure from the Articles, not an expression of them.

The Prayer Book

Cranmer’s liturgical genius gave the English-speaking church prayers of great beauty and precision. The Book of Common Prayer is not mere ceremony but teaching in the form of worship. Its collects — short, structured prayers — address God, recall his nature, make a petition, ground it in his character or Christ’s work, and end with praise to the Trinity. “Almighty God, unto whom all hearts be open, all desires known, and from whom no secrets are hid” is the doctrine of God’s knowledge on the lips of the congregation. Its General Confession — “we have left undone those things which we ought to have done; and we have done those things which we ought not to have done” — searches the conscience more deeply than many modern confessions.

The pattern of the early church shaped Cranmer’s services: “they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers” (Acts 2:42). The daily offices of Morning and Evening Prayer, praying through the Psalms and the lectionary, embody the conviction of Hebrews 10:24–25 that gathered worship is essential life, and that as the Day draws near the rhythm should quicken. And Cranmer put doxology at the heart of worship, because every encounter with God’s truth should end as Paul’s argument in Romans does: “Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Romans 11:33).

Bishops

Anglicanism keeps the historic threefold order of deacon, priest and bishop. For many Anglicans this is a matter of church order, good for the church’s wellbeing rather than essential to its being. For Anglo-Catholics it is essential. Evangelical Anglicans tend to hold it lightly, putting the gospel above the structure.

Its best figures

At its best the tradition has produced towering figures: Cranmer, martyred for the faith; the Caroline divines such as Lancelot Andrewes; the evangelicals of the eighteenth-century revival, George Whitefield, John Newton and William Wilberforce; and in the twentieth century J. I. Packer, John Stott and Alister McGrath.

Stott’s The Cross of Christ (1986) is arguably the finest twentieth-century treatment of the atonement in English. His exposition of penal substitution, written for a generation embarrassed by it, is historically careful and pastorally luminous. Stott was Anglican to his bones — liturgical, ordered, shaped by the Prayer Book — and thoroughly evangelical.

Unity and today

Anglicanism’s instinct to hold diverse traditions together has always looked to Christ’s prayer “that they may all be one” (John 17:21). That unity is not organisational merger but union in him. Packer argued throughout his life that evangelicals of different traditions should find their deepest unity in the gospel of Christ crucified, risen and reigning, and work outward from that centre.

The Episcopal Church in the United States and the Anglican Church in North America represent different expressions of the tradition; the latter was formed largely by those determined to keep orthodox Anglican theology in the face of revision in the mainline.

For reflection

What could you learn from the shape of Cranmer’s collects about how to pray? Pray the General Confession slowly this week. Why does it matter that the Articles, not later diversity, define historic Anglicanism?

4.title: Baptist
4.essay:
The Baptist tradition emerged in the early seventeenth century from the English Separatists. Its founders were convinced that the New Testament pattern — a gathered community of visible believers — had been obscured by the parish system and by infant baptism. If baptism is the sign of the new covenant, they argued, it belongs to those who have personally entered that covenant by faith.

Confessions and family

The key confessions are the First London Confession (1644), the Second London Confession (1689), which closely follows Westminster, and the New Hampshire Confession (1833). The 1689 Confession shows how thoroughly Reformed early English Baptists were: the doctrines of grace, covenant theology — with the crucial difference that the new covenant community is made up of believers only — and a high view of Scripture.

The family is vast: Reformed Baptists, heirs of 1689; Southern Baptists, the largest Protestant denomination in the United States; General Baptists, who are Arminian; independent fundamentalist Baptists; and many more. Charles Spurgeon, John Bunyan, John Piper, Al Mohler and Mark Dever show the range of the tradition within a shared commitment to believer’s baptism and congregational government.

Four commitments

Baptist distinctives cluster around four commitments. Soul liberty: each person answers directly to God for their beliefs, with no coercion in religion. Believer’s baptism by immersion. The priesthood of all believers. And local church autonomy: the congregation stands under Christ, not under a bishop or presbytery.

Baptism

In the Great Commission, “make disciples” is the main verb; baptising and teaching describe how disciples are made (Matthew 28:19). On the Baptist reading, baptism follows discipleship; it does not begin it. And burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4) are best pictured by going under the water and coming up out of it. Baptism is more than a personal testimony: it is a sign and seal of union with Christ, and the believer’s first public act of obedience. It does not convey grace automatically; it signs and seals grace received by faith.

That conviction has propelled an extraordinary missionary movement. From William Carey, “the father of modern missions”, to Adoniram Judson and Lottie Moon, Baptists have shown that believer’s baptism goes hand in hand with the widest missionary vision.

Priests and congregations

The priesthood of all believers rests on texts like 1 Peter 2:9: “you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood”. It does not mean every Christian is their own pope, but that every believer has direct access to God through Christ and a priestly calling to worship, pray, witness and pray for others. Baptists became early champions of lay ministry, small-group Bible study and every-member evangelism.

And “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). Christ’s presence is not mediated through a line of bishops; it is given wherever his people gather in his name. You do not need a cathedral or a thousand people to have a real church. That is why Baptist churches multiply so readily in living rooms, school halls and shopfronts. The local church, under Christ and governed by its members with elders leading, is the primary expression of the church.

Religious liberty

Baptists were pioneers of religious freedom, suffering imprisonment in England for their conviction that coerced faith is no faith at all. Roger Williams founded Rhode Island on that principle, and Baptists became natural advocates of the separation of church and state at the American founding.

Spurgeon and Bunyan

Charles Haddon Spurgeon, “the Prince of Preachers”, preached to some five or six thousand people every Sunday at the Metropolitan Tabernacle in London. His theology was thoroughly Calvinistic and his preaching passionately evangelistic. He refused to choose between doctrinal precision and gospel urgency; because he trusted the Spirit to apply the word, the most Calvinistic preacher of his day was also its most earnest evangelist.

John Bunyan began The Pilgrim’s Progress in Bedford jail, imprisoned for preaching without a licence. Its power comes from his own journey — the Slough of Despond, the burden of sin, the cross where the burden falls off, the Celestial City. Bunyan was not so much writing theology as bleeding it onto the page. That is the Baptist tradition at its best: truth embodied in life, and life turned into proclamation.

For reflection

Why do Baptists insist that baptism follows faith? How does the priesthood of all believers change what you expect of yourself in your church? What can every tradition learn from Spurgeon’s refusal to choose between doctrine and urgency?

5.title: Methodist
5.essay:
Methodism began in 1738 not as a new denomination but as a renewal movement within the Church of England. At Oxford, John and Charles Wesley, later joined by George Whitefield, led the “Holy Club”, a disciplined band of students devoted to Scripture, prayer, fasting, visiting prisoners and works of mercy. “Methodist” was a taunt: these men were methodical about their faith.

Holiness

“For this is the will of God, your sanctification” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). Wesley seized on texts like this to insist that God means his people to be holy — not only declared righteous but actually made holy. “Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without which no one will see the Lord” (Hebrews 12:14). The tradition has kept that verse before a church tempted to let justification swallow sanctification. Holiness is not a second condition added to faith, but the necessary direction of a justified life.

Wesley’s best-known teaching is entire sanctification, or Christian perfection: the conviction that the Spirit can so work in a believer as to cleanse the heart of its ruling desire to sin, enabling wholehearted love for God and neighbour. It is not sinless perfection in an absolute sense, and Wesley framed it entirely by the two great commandments (Matthew 22:37–39). He drew on early Eastern writers as well as Western Protestants. The Reformed tradition agrees that sanctification is central but denies that it can be “entire” in this life. Still, the Wesleyan emphasis is a healthy rebuke to evangelicals who are comfortable with justification by faith and uncomfortable with real, visible holiness. Is my life growing in love for God and neighbour, or contracting around myself?

Arminian convictions

Wesley’s Arminianism sets him apart from the Reformed. He taught prevenient grace: the fall left humanity unable to seek God, but God’s Spirit works in every heart, restoring the will’s capacity to accept or reject the gospel. This is not the same as Reformed common grace; it is a saving, preparatory grace, and it is the Arminian answer to total depravity. He held that election rests on foreseen faith, and that a true believer can fall away from grace.

Wesley and Calvin could both quote Romans 8:29 and agree on its destination: conformity to the image of Christ. They differed over whether “foreknew” means God’s unconditional choice or his foreknowledge of faith. On many things — Scripture’s authority, Christ’s atoning death, the necessity of new birth, the urgency of holiness — they walk side by side. Wesley and Whitefield remained close friends despite their disagreement, a model of evangelical partnership across Reformed and Arminian lines.

Sources of theology

The “Wesleyan Quadrilateral” — a term coined later by Albert Outler — describes theological reflection drawing on Scripture, tradition, reason and experience, with Scripture as the primary authority. Reformed theology affirms Scripture’s primacy but is more cautious about experience as a source. Wesley’s teaching on a second work of grace became the mother of the Holiness movement and, indirectly, of Pentecostalism.

Social holiness

“The gospel of Christ knows of no religion but social; no holiness but social holiness,” Wesley wrote. He founded schools for miners’ children, dispensaries for the poor and loan funds for the unemployed. He preached in fields because the working poor rarely came to church, and rode some quarter of a million miles on horseback over fifty years. His last known letter urged William Wilberforce on against the slave trade. You cannot love God and ignore your neighbour; social holiness is not a liberal add-on but a Wesleyan non-negotiable. His life rebukes any Christianity that retreats into private piety and calls it faithfulness.

Charles Wesley’s hymns

Charles Wesley wrote over six thousand hymns, among the richest bodies of hymnody in English: “And Can It Be”, “Hark! the Herald Angels Sing”, “O for a Thousand Tongues to Sing”. They are not pious ditties but sung theology. Whatever our differences, we are all in his debt every time we open a hymnbook.

For reflection

Where has Wesley’s call to real holiness challenged you? How do Reformed and Wesleyan Christians differ on grace, and where do they agree? What would “social holiness” look like in your own neighbourhood? Sing or read “And Can It Be” this week.

6.title: Brethren
6.essay:
The Brethren movement emerged in Dublin and Plymouth in the late 1820s among devout Anglicans convinced that the institutional church had wandered from New Testament simplicity and that no denomination could contain the whole people of God. Their answer was radical: meet as a gathered company of believers, with no ordained clergy, no fixed liturgy and no denominational structure — just believers around the open Bible and the Lord’s Table.

Breaking bread

The Brethren built their weekly communion on texts like Acts 20:7: “On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread”. The Lord’s Day was the day of gathering, and the gathering centred on the bread. They believed the institutional church had buried the Supper under layers of ceremony, and they recovered its simplicity: believers gathered, bread broken, Christ remembered.

The Supper is a proclamation: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). “Until he comes” gives it a forward-looking charge, the church’s enacted cry of “Maranatha” — “Our Lord, come!” The Brethren’s longing for Christ’s return and their love of the Supper are fired by the same hope. Whether or not weekly communion is the only faithful practice, the instinct to centre worship on the cross is profoundly right.

Every-member ministry

The Brethren rejected a paid, ordained clergy on the ground that the New Testament knows no clergy–laity divide. Every believer is a priest (1 Peter 2:9) and gifted by the Spirit for the body (1 Corinthians 12). In the meeting any brother might be moved to pray, read Scripture, give thanks or preach. Their meetings, sometimes large and sometimes a dozen people in a living room, made no apology for simplicity: “where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). The grandeur is not in the setting but in the one who is present.

The tradition that rejected an academic clergy produced one of the most respected New Testament scholars of the twentieth century, F. F. Bruce, whose commentaries on Acts, Romans, Hebrews and others shaped a generation. The Spirit gives gifts as he wills.

Darby and dispensationalism

John Nelson Darby (1800–1882), the movement’s most prolific theologian, developed from his study of prophecy what became known as dispensationalism: God has worked in distinct dispensations; Israel and the church are two distinct peoples with distinct destinies; the church is a “parenthesis” in God’s programme for Israel, which will resume in the tribulation and millennium; and the church will be raptured before Daniel’s seventieth week. Through the Scofield Reference Bible and later Dallas Theological Seminary, it became the dominant view of the end times in American evangelicalism for much of the twentieth century. Reformed readers rightly see instead one people of God in Christ, and one visible return of Christ to judge and renew all things. The studies on Dispensational Distinctives and Covenant Theology set this out fully.

George Müller

George Müller (1805–1898), who stood with the Open Brethren against Darby in the split of 1848, embodied Brethren spirituality at its best. He cared for over ten thousand orphans in Bristol and received nearly a million and a half pounds for the work without ever making a public appeal. He told God and waited. His watchword was Psalm 81:10: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.” He kept meticulous journals of answered prayer for seventy years and published them so that others might see that the God of the Bible is the God of today.

This was not a prosperity gospel. Müller lived simply, gave generously and trusted God for the rest — the Sermon on the Mount applied to an institution. His journals are a running commentary on Philippians 4:19: “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.”

The gift

The Brethren gave the church a gift of recovered simplicity — the weekly breaking of bread, every-member ministry, and personal Bible study at the centre of the Christian life — that has shaped far more of evangelicalism than those who know the name might suppose.

For reflection

What would it look like to centre your church’s worship more clearly on the cross? How does Müller’s life challenge your prayers about money and provision? Why do Reformed Christians differ from Darby on Israel and the church?

7.title: Pentecostal & Charismatic
7.essay:
In April 1906, in a run-down former church building on Azusa Street in Los Angeles, a Black Holiness preacher named William J. Seymour began services that would ignite one of the most significant movements in church history. Today Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity, broadly defined, is the fastest-growing part of world Christianity, numbering in the hundreds of millions.

From the margins

That the revival began under a one-eyed son of former slaves, in an era of rigid segregation, was itself a sign. Azusa Street was deliberately interracial; Frank Bartleman famously said, “The color line was washed away in the blood.” The movement’s origin among the poor and powerless fits the Spirit’s pattern: “God chose what is foolish in the world to shame the wise” (1 Corinthians 1:27).

What Pentecostals believe

Pentecostalism grew out of the Wesleyan Holiness tradition and its doctrine of a “second blessing” after conversion. Pentecostals identified that blessing as baptism in the Holy Spirit, shown first by speaking in tongues, as at Pentecost: “And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:4). They hold that all the gifts of 1 Corinthians 12–14 — tongues, interpretation, prophecy, healing, miracles, words of knowledge and wisdom — remain normative today.

The charismatic movement, from the 1960s, brought Pentecostal gifts and expectations into mainline Protestant, Catholic and eventually Reformed churches, often without the teaching that tongues are the initial evidence; charismatics speak more broadly of being filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18) again and again. The “Third Wave” of John Wimber and C. Peter Wagner widened it further.

What they have recovered

“To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good” (1 Corinthians 12:7). The charismatic movement has pressed on a sometimes unwilling church the truth that every believer is gifted and every gift is for others. A church that suppresses the ministry of its members is impoverished, and the wider church is better for having been reminded.

Pentecostal spirituality is marked by earnest, expectant asking, resting on the Father’s generosity: “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). Reformed and charismatic Christians can pray that text together. And at Pentecost Peter said, “this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16): God would pour out his Spirit “on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (Joel 2:28) — not only on kings, priests and prophets, but on every member of his people. That we live in the age of the Spirit’s lavish outpouring is not in dispute.

Pentecostal and charismatic worship is marked by spontaneity, emotional expressiveness, extended singing, prayer in tongues and expectation that the Spirit will move. It has profoundly shaped contemporary evangelical worship, for good and for ill. At its most careful it looks like Jack Hayford of The Church on the Way, whose worship was deeply trinitarian and reverent; his song “Majesty” captures the instinct at its finest: the Spirit’s presence does not compete with the Father’s majesty or the Son’s lordship but exalts them.

Where we differ

Reformed theologians, and many continuationists such as Wayne Grudem, hold that Spirit baptism is the same as the new birth — “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13) — and that Pentecost, like the resurrection, is a historical, unrepeatable event rather than a pattern for every believer.

On the gifts themselves, the debate between cessationists and continuationists is genuine, and serious scholars of deep learning and piety reach different conclusions. Wayne Grudem’s The Gift of Prophecy and D. A. Carson’s Showing the Spirit are careful continuationist-leaning treatments; Richard Gaffin’s Perspectives on Pentecost is a careful cessationist one. Weighing the texts, the cessationist position is the more faithful. The revelatory and sign gifts attested the apostles and their message (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), and once the foundation was laid (Ephesians 2:20) they ceased. The Spirit’s work of conviction, illumination, gifting for service and answering prayer goes on undiminished. And this is held with charity toward continuationist brothers and sisters.

In your church

Many in your congregation may have been shaped by the charismatic movement and cherish the experience of the Spirit’s immediate presence and power. That presence and power are real, whatever our conclusions about particular gifts. Every Christian is a post-Pentecost Christian, and that changes everything.

For reflection

What has the charismatic movement rightly recovered for the whole church? How would you explain, graciously, why you hold the view you do on the gifts? Pray Luke 11:13 for yourself and your church this week.

8.title: Roman Catholic
8.essay:
Roman Catholicism is the largest Christian body in the world, with over 1.3 billion members — roughly half of all Christians. Its history is the history of the Western church from the apostles through the Council of Trent, the Counter-Reformation and the two Vatican Councils to the present.

What the Reformation was about

The Reformation was not first a protest against corruption, though corruption was real. It was a protest against the medieval church’s teaching on salvation. Luther’s question was not, “How do I find a moral church?” but, “How do I find a gracious God?” The Catholic and Protestant answers differ at the deepest level: on justification, on the authority of Scripture, and on how grace reaches us.

Justification

Catholic teaching holds that justification involves both the forgiveness of sins and the inner transformation of the person by infused grace — a process of becoming righteous. The justified person cooperates with grace and can merit further grace and eternal life. That righteousness is nourished through seven sacraments — baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders and marriage — administered by the ordained priesthood.

Paul’s argument runs the other way: “Now to the one who works, his wages are not counted as a gift but as his due. And to the one who does not work but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:4–5). Justification works by the logic of gift, not wages. God justifies the ungodly — not the nearly righteous, not the sufficiently repentant — by crediting to them a righteousness that is entirely Christ’s. Paul excludes works from the ground of salvation so thoroughly that his language becomes almost repetitive: “not your own doing … not a result of works, so that no one may boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9). He affirms the good works that follow (Ephesians 2:10), but not as part of the basis. The difference is not whether transformation happens — Protestants insist it does, in sanctification — but whether it is part of justification.

The Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999), between Catholics and Lutherans, found significant common ground. But the role of merit and the sufficiency of Christ’s righteousness remain unresolved.

Scripture and tradition

Catholicism holds that revelation comes through Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition together, both interpreted by the Magisterium — the teaching office of the Pope and the bishops in union with him. The church also defined the canon, including the deuterocanonical books. Protestants hold to sola Scriptura: Scripture is the supreme, sufficient and self-authenticating word of God, the judge of all tradition. That is not a denial that tradition exists, but an insistence that it stands under Scripture, not alongside it.

One mediator, one sacrifice

“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5). The word “one” does the work. Catholic teaching on Mary — the Immaculate Conception, the Assumption, titles such as Mediatrix — and on the saints as intercessors, with prayers addressed to them, departs from the New Testament pattern of direct access to the Father through Christ alone. Catholics distinguish veneration from worship, but Protestants regard prayer to the departed as contrary to Scripture’s teaching on the sole mediation of Christ.

And “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). He sat down because the work was finished. The Catholic doctrine of the Mass — that the Eucharist re-presents Christ’s sacrifice in an unbloody manner — sits uneasily with that finality. The Reformed Supper is a feeding on Christ by faith through the Spirit, a remembrance and proclamation, but not a sacrifice.

What we honour

Evangelical response must be clear and charitable. We differ on questions the Reformers rightly called essential. But the Catholic tradition has preserved and passed on the Trinitarian and Christological faith of the early councils; it has produced saints, scholars and martyrs of great devotion; and it is the home in which many in our congregations were nurtured.

Augustine was claimed by both sides at the Reformation. Luther and Calvin drew heavily on his writings against Pelagius, with their sovereignty of grace; Trent also claimed him, read through Aquinas. Both were right that he shaped them, and both emphasised different parts of a vast body of work.

Catholic family and friends

Many believers have Catholic spouses, parents, children or siblings for whom the church is home. The pastoral task is not to hand people a refutation kit but to give them a deep enough grasp of the gospel to speak it lovingly and clearly. A Catholic family member needs to hear what imputed righteousness means: that their standing before God rests entirely on Christ’s finished work, not on any cooperation of their own. That is news worth announcing gently and persistently. The Evangelism study’s chapter on Roman Catholic friends offers more help.

For reflection

Why was Luther’s question about a gracious God, not a moral church, at the heart of the Reformation? How would you explain Romans 4:4–5 to a Catholic friend? What has the Catholic tradition preserved that we should be thankful for?

9.title: Eastern Orthodox
9.essay:
The Great Schism of 1054 divided the church into West and East, a division never formally healed. Eastern Orthodoxy is a family of self-governing national churches — Greek, Russian, Serbian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Antiochian and others — united by a common theology, liturgy and spirituality rooted in the Greek-speaking church of the East.

Ancient and beautiful

To meet Orthodoxy is to meet something ancient, dense and beautiful. The Divine Liturgy of John Chrysostom has been sung in substantially the same form for well over a thousand years. Orthodox theology is shaped above all by the seven ecumenical councils, from Nicaea in 325 to the second council of Nicaea in 787, which defined the doctrine of the Trinity and of Christ against Arianism, Nestorianism, Monophysitism and iconoclasm. Orthodoxy sees itself as the guardian of that conciliar faith, unchanged.

The filioque controversy — whether the Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, as the East holds, or from the Father and the Son, as the West confesses — was a major cause of the schism and remains unresolved.

Theosis

The defining Orthodox concept is theosis, or deification. Salvation is participation in the divine nature, and the goal of the Christian life is union with God. The text it rests on is 2 Peter 1:4: “so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature”. Athanasius put it famously: “He was made man that we might be made God” — not dissolving into God, which would be pantheism, but sharing in his life, love and holiness.

Protestants have often been nervous of this language, fearing it blurs the line between Creator and creature. But the text is in Scripture, and it speaks of something real. Reformed theology affirms the substance: the Spirit lives in believers and conforms them to the image of Christ, filling them with a love and holiness that are truly God’s own, shared and not manufactured. The difference lies in how this relates to justification, and in the role of the sacraments and ascetic disciplines.

Western Christians, Protestant and Catholic alike, have often found in Orthodoxy a corrective to an overly legal, transactional picture of salvation — a reminder that the gospel is not only about legal standing but about union with the living God. Christ prayed “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us” (John 17:21). No tradition has meditated more deeply on that mutual indwelling, and the church is poorer if it does not listen.

The unknowable God

Orthodox theology is characteristically apophatic: God in his essence is utterly beyond human categories. We know him not in his essence but in his energies — his actions and self-giving in creation and redemption. This distinction, developed by Gregory Palamas in the fourteenth century, has no exact parallel in Western thought.

It goes with an aching longing for God himself, not only his gifts: “As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God. My soul thirsts for God, for the living God” (Psalm 42:1–2). Every encounter leaves the soul hungrier. That is not immaturity; it is the shape of love for an infinite God.

Worship and icons

The Divine Liturgy is shaped as a participation in the worship of heaven in Revelation 4–5, where the living creatures never cease to say, “Holy, holy, holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” (Revelation 4:8). Earthly worship joins the heavenly song. Whatever our liturgical differences, that instinct is deeply biblical: worship is not a performance for a human audience but participation in the song of heaven.

Icons, for the Orthodox, are not idols but windows into heaven: images of Christ and the saints that are venerated, not worshipped. The seventh council defended them against the iconoclasts, arguing that to deny Christ can be depicted is to deny the reality of his incarnation. Reformed theology, following the second commandment, rejects images in worship — a point of significant ongoing disagreement.

Athanasius against the world

At Nicaea and for decades afterwards, Athanasius of Alexandria stood almost alone for the full deity of Christ against the Arians. Exiled five times by four emperors, he refused to compromise the confession that the Son is of the same substance as the Father. “Athanasius against the world” sums up his life: the truth of who Christ is mattered more to him than comfort, office or safety. Orthodoxy treasures him, and so should we all.

In the twentieth century Alexander Schmemann’s For the Life of the World presented the Eucharist as the place where heaven and earth meet and the new creation breaks into the old. Whatever our differences on the Supper, his insistence that gathered worship is a foretaste of the kingdom’s banquet is a gift to the whole church.

For reflection

What does 2 Peter 1:4 add to your picture of salvation? How might the Orthodox longing for God himself deepen your prayer? Why do Reformed Christians reject icons in worship, and how would you explain that respectfully?

10.title: Anabaptist & Mennonite
10.essay:
The Anabaptist movement arose in Zurich in 1525, alongside but sharply distinct from the Lutheran and Reformed Reformations. Conrad Grebel, Felix Manz and George Blaurock gathered for an unauthorised baptism of adults, starting a movement that Zwingli, Luther and Calvin alike condemned as dangerous radicalism.

Re-baptisers

“Anabaptist” means re-baptiser, and it was a term of contempt. These believers denied the validity of infant baptism and insisted that only a conscious, voluntary confession of faith could come before the sign of the covenant. Their vision was a gathered church of the born-again: a community visibly distinct from the surrounding society, living out the Sermon on the Mount, practising mutual accountability and refusing all compromise with state power.

The Dutch leader Menno Simons (1496–1561) gave his name to the stream that survived, the Mennonites. Later came the Amish (Jakob Ammann, 1693) and the communal Hutterites. Through a complex and debated genealogy, the Baptists share their believer’s baptism while rejecting their pacifism and separatism.

Believer’s baptism

Anabaptists read the Great Commission as the charter of believer’s baptism: make disciples, then baptise (Matthew 28:19). To baptise infants who cannot yet be disciples is, on this reading, to reverse the order Christ gave. Paedobaptists answer that the pattern of Abraham’s household, where circumcision came before conscious faith, points the other way. The debate is genuine and has divided Bible-saturated believers for five centuries. Weighing it, believer’s baptism is the more faithful reading: the new covenant is made with those in whom the law is written and who all know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:33–34), and baptism is its sign, given to those who have entered it by faith.

For Anabaptists, infant baptism was more than a mistake; it was the support beam of Christendom’s confusion of church and state.

The sword and the cross

“But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39). Anabaptists take Jesus at his word here with a literalness the Reformers resisted. The Reformers used a two-kingdoms distinction: as a private person, a Christian may not resist evil, but as a magistrate or soldier he must restrain it for the common good. The Anabaptist reply was that Christ’s ethic knows no such division. Christians do not hold public office, swear oaths or bear arms. The church is a colony of heaven in enemy territory, not a force for reforming earthly institutions. The cross, not the sword, is the Christian’s weapon.

The ban

Formal excommunication of the unrepentant — “Purge the evil person from among you” (1 Corinthians 5:13) — was central to Anabaptist church life and a constant source of controversy. Menno Simons applied it even to the spouses of the excommunicated, severely enough to split Anabaptism itself. Yet the instinct is sound: a visible community of the regenerate needs visible discipline. A church that never excludes anyone has effectively admitted that membership means nothing. The Reformers agreed on the principle and differed on its severity.

Martyrs

For their convictions Anabaptists were drowned, burned and beheaded by Catholic, Lutheran and Reformed authorities alike — one of the great shames of Reformation history. Felix Manz was drowned in Zurich’s river in 1527, with Zwingli’s backing. That same year the first Anabaptist confession, the Schleitheim Confession, set out seven articles: believer’s baptism, the ban, the Lord’s Supper as a memorial, separation from the world, pastors in the church, rejection of the sword, and rejection of oaths. Radical, costly and coherent.

The martyrs read Revelation as their book: “Here is a call for the endurance of the saints, those who keep the commandments of God and their faith in Jesus” (Revelation 14:12). The Martyrs’ Mirror (1660), a vast account of Christian martyrs from Stephen onward, preserved their testimonies: men and women who sang psalms on the way to execution, forgave their killers and refused to recant. In many Mennonite homes it stood second only to the Bible. Whatever our disagreements, their blood demands respect. They died for Christ.

Today

The Mennonite Central Committee is one of the most respected relief organisations in the world, working in more than fifty countries. The Anabaptist theology of service — witness not by sword or coin but by presence and help — has produced a practice of mission many evangelicals have come to admire. And their insistence on costly discipleship, not cheap grace, still searches the whole church.

For reflection

Where do you agree and disagree with the Anabaptist reading of Matthew 5:39? Why does a church need visible discipline? What does the courage of the Anabaptist martyrs say to Christians who face pressure today?

11.title: Congregationalist
11.essay:
Congregationalism arose in Elizabethan England among Puritan dissenters who believed the Reformation had not gone far enough. In the 1580s Robert Browne, Henry Barrow and John Greenwood argued that the true church is a gathered, covenanted congregation of visible saints, not a parish of everyone who happens to live within its boundaries.

Pilgrims and Puritans

Each local congregation, they held, governs itself under Christ, with no bishop, presbytery or synod above it. The Pilgrim Fathers who sailed on the Mayflower in 1620 were Congregationalists, Separatists fleeing persecution to plant a covenant community in New England. Before landing at Plymouth they signed the Mayflower Compact, a civic covenant modelled on their church covenant, establishing government by mutual consent for the common good — often called a seed of American self-government. The Great Migration of the 1630s brought thousands more and founded Massachusetts Bay Colony, which John Winthrop called “a city upon a hill”.

Thoroughly Reformed

Congregationalism produced some of the greatest preachers and theologians in English and American history: John Owen, Thomas Goodwin, Isaac Watts and Jonathan Edwards. Its theology is fully Reformed — Calvinist in its teaching on salvation and covenantal in its reading of Scripture — while insisting that the local church is the basic unit of church government.

The Savoy Declaration of 1658, drawn up by an assembly including Owen and Goodwin, adopted the Westminster Confession almost word for word, replacing only its chapters on presbyterian government with congregational ones. It shows that the Reformed consensus was broader than any one form of church government.

The gathered church

“For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them” (Matthew 18:20). Congregationalists find here the charter of the gathered, self-governing church. Christ’s presence is promised to the assembly gathered in his name, however small. That is not a consolation prize for small congregations; it is the definition of the church. Where the word is preached, believers are gathered in Christ’s name and discipline is exercised under his authority, there is the church in its fullness. Owen gave this conviction its fullest defence.

Membership is visible, voluntary and accountable. Each congregation is founded on a church covenant: a mutual pledge before God to walk together in the ways of Christ, submit to Scripture, care for one another and keep discipline.

The keys

Congregationalists read the “keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:19) as given neither to Peter alone, nor to a line of bishops, nor to the eldership only, but to the gathered congregation. The power to bind and loose — to admit and exclude members — belongs to the assembled church acting under Christ. Owen developed this carefully in The True Nature of a Gospel Church. Elders lead, but the members hold final authority in discipline, doctrine and government.

Sending and stirring

At Antioch, while the church was worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them” (Acts 13:2). The church sent its two best leaders — not at Jerusalem’s direction, but at the Spirit’s call, discerned and confirmed by the gathered community. Congregationalists see here the pattern of a missionary church: Spirit-led, congregationally affirmed and locally accountable.

And “let us consider how to stir up one another to love and good works” (Hebrews 10:24). Not a pastor stirring a passive flock, but members engaged in each other’s growth. The gathered assembly is not an audience but a community of mutual responsibility.

Jonathan Edwards

The greatest theologian America has produced was a Congregationalist pastor in Northampton, Massachusetts. Jonathan Edwards’s preaching sparked the Northampton revival of 1734–35, and he became the leading theologian of the Great Awakening that followed. His Religious Affections remains among the most penetrating studies of what genuine conversion looks and feels like, and of its counterfeits.

For reflection

What would it mean for your church to see itself as a covenanted community rather than an audience? Who should hold the “keys” — elders, congregation, or both? How does Acts 13:1–3 shape the way a church sends missionaries?

12.title: Oriental Orthodox
12.essay:
The Oriental Orthodox churches — Coptic in Egypt, Ethiopian and Eritrean, Armenian, Syriac, and Malankara in India — are among the oldest Christian communities in the world. The Coptic Church claims Mark the Evangelist as its founder. Armenia was the first nation to adopt Christianity as its state religion, traditionally in 301. And the Ethiopian church cherishes a link with the official baptised by Philip.

The Ethiopian on the road

In Acts 8 an Ethiopian court official was reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot, and Philip, “beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus” (Acts 8:35). Whether or not an institutional line can be drawn, the spiritual claim is profound: the gospel reached Africa in the apostolic age, carried by a man who met Christ in the scroll of Isaiah. The Ethiopian church has read Isaiah 53 as its own story ever since.

Miaphysite, not Monophysite

These churches parted from the rest of Christendom at the Council of Chalcedon in 451, refusing its formula of Christ “in two natures”. They are often called Monophysite, a term they reject. Their theologians prefer “Miaphysite”: after the incarnation Christ has one united nature, divine and human, without confusion, mixture, separation or change. They insist this is not a denial of his full humanity but a different way of framing the same orthodox conviction. The difference from Chalcedonian Christianity may be more a matter of terms than substance, and modern dialogue has produced several joint declarations suggesting substantial agreement.

Ancient worship and the desert

Their liturgies are extraordinarily old — the Coptic Liturgy of St Basil, the Armenian Badarak, the Ethiopian liturgy in Ge’ez — preserving forms of worship from the early centuries. The sense of standing in an unbroken chain of prayer reaching back toward the apostles is profound.

These churches are also the cradle of Christian monasticism. Anthony of Egypt (251–356) and Pachomius began the movement that spread through the whole church, and the sayings of the Desert Fathers shaped Christian spirituality for centuries. Athanasius’s Life of Anthony became one of the most widely read books of the ancient church. Augustine heard its story in Milan shortly before his conversion, and it drove him into the garden where he took up and read Romans 13.

Where we differ

In Oriental Orthodox theology, as in Eastern Orthodoxy, the authority of tradition stands alongside Scripture. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church has the largest canon of any Christian body, 81 books, including texts not found in Catholic, Orthodox or Protestant Bibles. Reformed Christians hold Scripture alone as the supreme rule, and the Protestant canon of sixty-six books.

Churches that know martyrdom

For most of their history these churches have survived as minorities under Islamic rule, often severely persecuted. In the Armenian Genocide of 1915–1923, about a million and a half Armenians were killed by the Ottoman state — the martyrdom of a nation. The Armenian Apostolic Church survived, as it had survived Persian, Byzantine, Arab, Mongol and Turkish persecution for seventeen centuries. Archbishop Grigoris Balakian’s memoir Armenian Golgotha is one of the great records of Christian suffering in the modern era.

The Coptic Church has kept the faith under Roman persecution, Byzantine harassment, Arab conquest, Ottoman rule and modern Islamist violence. In 2015, twenty-one men — twenty Copts and a Ghanaian companion — were beheaded on a Libyan beach, many dying with the name of Jesus on their lips. Pope Shenouda III (1971–2012) shepherded his flock through decades of persecution, exile and revival, while the Coptic diaspora planted churches across the world.

For these churches Romans 8 is not a text for comfortable Christians: “No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). It has been read at gravesides, in prison cells and during genocide. The churches that have lost the most and kept the faith know something about that passage that comfortable Christians do not.

Every tribe and tongue

Ge’ez, Armenian, Coptic, Syriac, Malayalam: these are languages and traditions the Western church has often barely noticed. Yet they will be there before the throne, “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages” (Revelation 7:9). John’s vision corrects every kind of narrowness, including Reformed narrowness. The catholic church is more glorious, more diverse and more ancient than any single tradition can contain.

For reflection

What does the long suffering of these churches teach you about faithfulness? How should Christians in comfortable places pray for persecuted churches? Read Revelation 7:9–17 and give thanks for believers you will one day worship beside.

13.title: Seventh-day Adventist
13.essay:
The Seventh-day Adventist Church grew out of the “Great Disappointment” of 1844, when William Miller’s prediction that Christ would return on 22 October failed. Rather than abandon the movement, a core group reinterpreted the prophecy.

Origins

1844, they concluded, marked not Christ’s return to earth but his entry into the Most Holy Place of the heavenly sanctuary to begin a work of “investigative judgment”. Around that reinterpretation, and guided decisively by the prophetic ministry of Ellen G. White (1827–1915), the church was formally organised in 1863. The Great Disappointment is a warning to every generation that sets dates: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows, not even the angels of heaven, nor the Son, but the Father only” (Matthew 24:36).

Its name carries its two most distinctive beliefs: worship on Saturday, the seventh day, and a strong emphasis on Christ’s imminent return. It is one of the fastest-growing Protestant bodies in the world, with about 21 million baptised members, strongest in Africa, Latin America and Southeast Asia. It runs one of the largest Protestant networks of hospitals and schools in the world, including Loma Linda University Health and AdventHealth. Its emphasis on health — no pork, alcohol or tobacco, and a preference for vegetarianism — produced the Kellogg cereal company, through John Harvey Kellogg, later expelled from the church, and some of the most studied long-lived communities in the world.

The Sabbath

Adventists base Saturday worship directly on the fourth commandment (Exodus 20:8–10), arguing that the seventh day is plainly Saturday and that no New Testament text transfers it to Sunday. In their sharper forms, they call Sunday worship a post-apostolic innovation or even part of the “mark of the beast” system, and read “those who keep the commandments of God” (Revelation 14:12) as those who keep the seventh-day Sabbath.

The best answer is that the Sabbath was a sign and shadow fulfilled in Christ, who is our rest (Matthew 11:28; Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10). The church gathers on the first day, the day of resurrection (Matthew 28:1; Mark 16:2), the Lord’s Day and the day of new creation (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10), as a gift rather than as a transferred Sabbath law. The Westminster Confession holds instead that the Sabbath was moved to the first day. This is a genuine exegetical debate. And Adventist seriousness about costly obedience is something the wider church can learn from.

Soul sleep

Adventists reject the natural immortality of the soul: the dead are unconscious until the resurrection. They read “the dead in Christ will rise first” (1 Thessalonians 4:16) and Jesus’ words about “all who are in the tombs” (John 5:28) in that light. It is a minority Protestant view, though not without defenders; William Tyndale appears to have held it.

The Reformed reply is that “sleep” is a picture of bodily death, while the believer’s spirit is with Christ: Paul’s desire was “to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Philippians 1:23), and to be “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). God “is not God of the dead, but of the living” (Matthew 22:32). Yet on the final hope we fully agree: salvation is not merely the immortality of the soul but the resurrection of the body.

Investigative judgment and Ellen White

Adventists teach that since 1844 Christ has been reviewing the records of all professing believers in the heavenly sanctuary to determine who is truly saved, a process that will end before his return. This teaching has no biblical warrant and has been widely criticised by evangelical scholars — even Walter Martin, who counted Adventists as fellow Christians, rejected it. It introduces a troubling uncertainty into assurance: am I converted enough to survive the investigation?

Ellen White’s writings are treated as “the Spirit of Prophecy”, a continuing gift that, while not equal to Scripture, functions as an authoritative interpreter of it. Reformed Christianity rejects this both because the revelatory gifts have ceased and because of the biblical test of a prophet: several of her specific predictions did not come to pass. Her most influential book, The Great Controversy (1888), tells the cosmic conflict between Christ and Satan, gives the Sabbath a central place, identifies the papacy with the beast of Revelation and predicts a final Sunday law. Whatever one thinks of its claims, it shows the power of a grand story to shape a community.

How to think of Adventists

Many Adventists hold firmly to the Trinity, the deity of Christ and salvation by grace through faith, and evangelicals such as Walter Martin counted them brothers and sisters despite serious errors. Others hold the distinctive teachings in ways that cloud the gospel. In conversation, start with the shared ground of Christ and his cross, and gently press the question of assurance: is my hope resting on Christ’s finished work, or on how I fare in a judgment still under way?

For reflection

Why is date-setting for Christ’s return so dangerous? How would you explain, graciously, why Christians gather on the first day? What does the doctrine of investigative judgment do to assurance, and how does the gospel answer it?
